LEARN VOID / 01

Syntax basics

Read your first VOID program.

Complete program for the synchronous entry adapter. The result below is the returned integer.

Read the function declaration

func entry(boxes: i32) -> i32: names a function, its integer input and its integer result. Here a box holds three items, so four boxes produce 12 items.

Use indentation for the body

The colon starts the body; indent its statements by four spaces. return boxes * 3 calculates and returns the item count. Ordinary blocks need no braces or statement-ending semicolons. A # comment explains the idea without affecting execution.

Understand the entry adapter

The current command-line adapter passes one i32 input to entry and displays its returned integer. The first example uses that adapter; the applications below use a separate execution mode. Neither supplies a printing API. Use descriptive lowercase snake_case names.

Choose an application entry point

For application execution, use voidc run main.void --app with a zero-argument synchronous main(). A main without a result exits successfully; a main returning i32 must return on every path. This short application deliberately returns status seven. That status belongs to the process and is not printed; standard output is empty. No numeric adapter input is passed.

Executable top-level statements are an alternative to main, not something to combine with it. This source executes in order and returns success when capacity is available. Run its filename with --app too.

Top-level fallthrough or a bare return means status zero. Top-level locals are not visible inside ordinary functions, and imported modules cannot contain executable statements. Async application entry and command-line argument APIs are not implemented.
